# The Economics of Artificial Intelligence

<p class="sx-lede">In 1589 Queen Elizabeth I refused a patent for a knitting machine because she feared it would turn her people into beggars. AI brings the same anxiety to a different kind of work.</p>

My entry to the Berkeley Economic Review High School Essay Contest. The prompt asked how AI may reshape demand for high-, middle- and low-skill workers in the United States, how that could affect wage inequality, and for one policy to help workers adapt.

::: {.sx-section}
<p class="sx-label">The prompt</p>

## "The Economics of Artificial Intelligence"

> Artificial intelligence is expected to affect workers differently across the skill distribution. Analyze how AI adoption may reshape labor demand for high-skill, middle-skill, and low-skill workers in the United States, considering both productivity-enhancing and displacement effects. Discuss how these impacts might influence wage inequality. Propose and critically evaluate one specific policy designed to help workers adapt to AI-driven changes.
:::

::: {.sx-section}
<p class="sx-label">The argument</p>

## AI is not a neutral force

Using the task-based model, which treats a job as a bundle of tasks, and the idea of skill-biased technological change, the essay argues that AI speeds up the polarisation of the labour market. It complements high-skill workers by automating the routine parts of their jobs, but a productivity gain is not the same as a pay rise: only workers whose judgement AI cannot replace capture the value. Middle-skill jobs such as accounting and paralegal work are rule-based, so AI substitutes for them directly. Low-skill manual jobs are hard to automate, yet they are exposed when displaced workers move into them. The result is a U-shaped labour market, a falling labour share of income and wider wage inequality.
:::

::: {.sx-section}
<p class="sx-label">The policies</p>

## Tax parity now, lifelong learning accounts for the long run

In the short term, the essay proposes tax parity: the US tax code taxes workers through payroll taxes while generous depreciation rules effectively subsidise automation, so firms are nudged towards replacing people. In the long term, it proposes lifelong learning accounts, so that retraining can keep pace with displacement.
:::
